attempts.entry_title: Short time-scale coding in rat S1 during whisker sequence discrimination (McGuire et al. 2016)
attempts.summary: Most main findings held up: rats judged whisker sequences by mean speed and treated FMS and SMF alike, S1 units split into Fast, Medium and Slow classes with the reported laminar pattern, Fast units tracked impulse velocity, L5 Slow Positive units signalled choice, and Fast and Medium units decoded the sequence. The choice decoder did not reproduce: Slow units predicted choice far above the paper's 65%, Fast and Medium units also well above chance, and the Methods leave open how it was trained. The one rat that told FMS from SMF is not deposited. Several class outcomes assume the dataset's stored modulated units are the paper's. Minor claims on baseline rates and latencies reproduced in part.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of McGuire, Telian, Laboy-Juarez et al. (2016) on CRCNS ssc-4, which holds the spike times and trial data of 80 recording sessions in the five recorded rats. It checks the behaviour of those rats, the unit counts, baseline rates, temporal modulation, impulse responses by layer, the regression on integrated panel speed that classes units as Fast, Medium, Slow Positive and Slow Negative, the responses and choice coding of each class, and the population decoders of stimulus and choice. Three claims are tested on the paper's supporting data.

notebooks.title: Behaviour, units, regression classes and responses (Figures 2 to 8)

outcomes.statement: All eight rats discriminated FFF from SSS but treated FMS and SMF as equivalent and intermediate; seven of eight showed no difference between FMS and SMF, and one rat (62SC) made more right choices to FMS than to SMF.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral Discrimination of FFF, FMS, SMF, and SSS Sequences, paragraph 3; Figure 2A and 2B
outcomes.quote: Seven out of eight rats failed to differentiate at all between FMS from SMF stimuli (proportion test, Bonferroni-adjusted p -value >0.00625). One rat (62SC) showed modest but significant discrimination, with more right-side choices to FMS than SMF stimuli ( p = 0.0039).

statistics.about: FMS against SMF right-choice fraction, each of seven rats
FMS against SMF right-choice fraction, rat 62SC

outcomes.notes: The data set holds five of the eight rats (18FB, 18Ri, 18Ro, 62BS, 107St). In all five, FFF draws more right choices than SSS (0.537 to 0.698 against 0.234 to 0.390) and FMS and SMF lie between, and FMS against SMF is not significant at 0.00625 (smallest p 0.10 by the z test and 0.11 by the continuity-corrected chi-square, 62BS). Both trial readings select the same 14186 trials. Rat 62SC, the one the paper finds discriminating, is not in the data set, so that part cannot be tested; the criterion caps the outcome at partial for fewer than eight rats. The data set's per-rat means over sessions equal the S1 Data values for four rats and differ by up to 0.026 for 18FB.
deviations: Five of eight rats; the three behaviour-only rats are not deposited.

outcomes.statement: Rats trained on FFF-FMS-SMF-SSS discrimination for 14.2 days on average (s.d. 4.4, range 8 to 22).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral Discrimination of FFF, FMS, SMF, and SSS Sequences, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: After 14.2 ± 4.4 (standard deviation [s.d.]) (range: 8–22) d of training on FFF-FMS-SMF-SSS discrimination, all eight rats successfully discriminated FFF from SSS stimuli
outcomes.notes: Distinct recording dates per rat are 11 (18FB), 12 (18Ri, 107St), 19 (18Ro) and 20 (62BS); mean 14.8, s.d. 4.3. The mean and the maximum are within tolerance, the minimum (11) is not within 0.8 of 8. Counting sessions, which match the paper's 12-22 d of recording, gives 12 to 22, mean 16.0, and the minimum is still outside. The data set holds only the recording days of the five recorded rats, and the shortest-trained rats may be among the three not deposited.
deviations: Five of eight rats, and only days with a deposited recording session.

outcomes.statement: Relative right-port choice (fraction of right choices for a stimulus minus the mean over all stimuli) was strongly related to the mean speed of the sequence for all rats.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral Discrimination of FFF, FMS, SMF, and SSS Sequences, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: Right drink port choice was strongly related to mean sequence speed for all rats ( Fig 2C ).
outcomes.notes: For each of the five rats relative right choice orders FFF above FMS and SMF above SSS (reading a), and the Pearson correlation with Table 1 mean speed is 0.967 to 0.998 (reading b), under both trial readings. The S1 Data means of all eight rats give the same (r 0.967 to 0.995).
deviations: Five of eight rats in the data set; all eight shown from S1 Data as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Fixing the panel in place, with the piezo moving behind it, impaired FFF against SSS discrimination in all but one of six rats tested.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral Discrimination of FFF, FMS, SMF, and SSS Sequences, paragraph 4; Figure 2D; S2B Fig
outcomes.quote: Panel fixation strongly impaired behavioral discrimination in all but one rat

statistics.about: FFF minus SSS right-choice fraction, fixed-panel against normal sessions

outcomes.notes: Tested on S2 Data after a reader's answer to this attempt's question. The first run had the claim as data from the data set and recorded it as blocked (data_missing), since the data set holds only the four normal sequences and no fixed-panel session; the reader changed the claim to data elsewhere, on the per-rat S2B Fig values in S2 Data, and to a lower fixed-panel value in at least five of six rats. On those values fixed-panel discrimination (FFF minus SSS right-choice fraction) is lower than moving-panel discrimination in all six rats, by 0.067 (18Ri) to 0.374 (107SI). The paired t test gives p = 0.0120 with the rat at 0 kept (reading ii, the paper's 0.012), mean change -0.169 (95% CI -0.282 to -0.056), and p = 0.0308 without it (reading i), mean change -0.174 (-0.322 to -0.026), so the criterion holds under both readings. The Figure 2D d-prime from S1 Data is lower in all six rats too (p = 0.0051 and 0.0176). The moving-panel values of S2B differ from the Figure 2B means and from the data set's mean and last session for the six rats with the control, so they summarise sessions the data set does not hold. The statement's "all but one" (one rat not significantly impaired) cannot be tested from per-rat summaries; the lowest change is 18Ri's (0.067, d-prime 1.02 to 0.78).
deviations: The per-rat values of S2B Fig are taken from S2 Data as deposited; the single trials are not public, so the paper's computation of each value is not repeated.
outcomes.where: PLOS Biology supporting information of doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002549, S2 Data (XLSX, data for S2B Fig) and S1 Data (XLSX, data for Figure 2D)

outcomes.statement: Discrimination of FFF against SSS in normal sessions was modest, with d-prime from 0.5 to 1.5 across rats.
outcomes.source: Discussion, Behavioral Integration of Stimulus Sequences, paragraph 2; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: Task performance was relatively low (d-prime for FFF versus SSS: 0.5–1.5), as in a prior study [ 13 ]
outcomes.notes: Per-rat d-prime over pooled sessions (reading a) is 0.45 (18FB) to 1.09 (18Ro), and the mean of per-session values (reading b) 0.46 to 1.23. The lowest value is within tolerance of 0.5; the highest is below 1.35 under both readings. Of the three rats not deposited, two have the highest d-prime by the S1 Data means (62SS 1.32, 107Si 1.17).
deviations: Five of eight rats.
Rates of 0 or 1 in a session are moved by half a trial before the z transform, a standard choice.

outcomes.statement: Two rats discriminated FSFS from SFFS when the sequences differed in mean speed (70 and 69.2% correct) but not when mean speed was the same (52 and 53%), even after more than 20 days; d-prime was 1.02 against 0.12.
outcomes.source: Results, Discrimination of FSFS versus SFFS Sequences, paragraph 2; Figure 3B and 3C
outcomes.quote: Both rats consistently discriminated FSFS from SFFS when they had different mean speed (58B: 70 ± 1.5% correct, 60W: 69.2 ± 1.6%), but not when they had the same mean speed, even after >20 cumulative days of training (58B: 52 ± 0.8% correct; 60W: 53 ± 0.8% correct). This was evident in the d-prime measure of discrimination between FSFS and SFSF stimuli, which was 1.02 for different-intensity stimuli and 0.12 for same-intensity stimuli
outcomes.notes: From the per-session values of S1 Data, 58B is 69.98 +- 1.47% correct (13 sessions) and 60W 69.17 +- 1.57% (15) with different intensities, and 51.74 +- 0.81% (22) and 53.02 +- 0.82% (21) with the same intensity, with same-intensity sessions up to day 56 and 52. D-prime as the mean of the two rats (reading a) is 1.004 and 0.130; per rat 1.061 and 0.947, 0.168 and 0.093 (reading b, outside tolerance for single rats). All six values are within tolerance under reading a.
outcomes.where: PLOS Biology supporting information of doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002549, S1 Data (XLSX, data for Figure 3)

outcomes.statement: The recordings yielded 306 single units and 167 multi-unit clusters (473 units) over 80 sessions in five rats, 3.8 single units per session on average (range 0 to 11).
outcomes.source: Results, S1 Recordings during Behavioral Discrimination, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Spike sorting yielded 3.8 (range: 0–11) well-separated single units per recording session ( Fig 4B ). ... We obtained 306 single units and 167 multi-unit clusters (total: 473 units) across 80 recording sessions in five rats (18FB, 18Ri, 18Ro, 62BS, 107St)
outcomes.notes: 330 single units (257 RS, 73 FS) and 176 multi-unit clusters, 506 in all, over 80 sessions in five rats; 4.12 single units per session, 0 to 12. Each value is within its tolerance, but the total is 33 above the paper's 473. The descriptor says units in columns A1 and B2 are to be dropped using MapPosition, which the file lacks; leaving out the fifth electrode of 18FB and 18Ri gives 459, not 473. By the unit counts per layer and type of the paper's S1 Table, the 33 extra units are in L2/3 (4), L4 (8), L5a (15) and L5b (6), none in L6.

outcomes.statement: Mean firing rate in the 25-ms prestimulus baseline in the nose poke was 6 to 10 Hz across layers for RS units, 8 to 32 Hz for FS units, and higher for multi-unit clusters.
outcomes.source: Results, S1 Recordings during Behavioral Discrimination, paragraph 2; S1 Table
outcomes.quote: Mean firing rate during a 25-ms prestimulus baseline period in the nose poke was 6–10 Hz across layers for RS units, 8–32 Hz for FS units, and higher for multi-unit clusters ( S1 Table ).
outcomes.notes: Layer means of the 25-ms baseline over completed trials are 5.93 (L2/3) to 11.40 Hz (L5a) for RS single units and 7.59 (L2/3) to 30.18 Hz (L5b) for FS. The RS maximum is above 11 Hz; the other bounds are within tolerance. Multi-units are higher than RS in 5 of 5 layers and higher than both RS and FS in 4 of 5. With all trials the RS maximum is 11.49 Hz. The paper's S1 Table gives 6.0 to 10.8 Hz for RS (L5a 10.8 Hz over 68 units, against 77 here) and 7.9 to 31.6 Hz for FS; the data set's 33 extra units are all in L2/3 to L5b by the S1 Table counts, so they are a likely source of the difference.
deviations: All 506 deposited units, not the paper's 473.

The baseline is averaged over completed trials, while the criterion says all trials. With all trials RS layer means are 6.09 to 11.49 Hz and FS 7.80 to 29.93 Hz, shown as a variant, and the outcome is the same.

outcomes.statement: 305 of 473 units (63.5%) had firing rates significantly modulated in time during the nose poke period.
outcomes.source: Results, S1 Recordings during Behavioral Discrimination, paragraph 3; Methods, Temporal response modulation
outcomes.quote: Three hundred five out of 473 units (63.5%) showed significant temporal modulation.
outcomes.notes: With 0 to 180 ms after nose poke entry (reading a) 310 of 506 units (61.3%) are modulated; with 0 to 180 ms after onset (reading b) 261 (51.6%). The two statistics the criterion names give the same p-value under uniform permutation, so they are one reading. The data set's stored p-values also mark 310 units, but they agree with reading a unit by unit for 73.1% (Spearman r of the p-values 0.60). They were computed over -50 to 300 ms (TempSig.Params); that window gives 363 units here (81.6% agreement), and a null that shuffles each trial's 10-ms bins gives 365 on that window (82.0%) and 321 on the Methods' window (73.7%), so the authors' test is not repeated exactly. The claims that depend on this one use the stored set, which the descriptor names as the paper's units, with reading a as a variant.
deviations: 506 units in the denominator, not 473.
Spikes are permuted uniformly within the window on each trial (the criterion's standard choice), drawn as a multinomial over the pooled bins, which is the same null.
A second null, shuffling each trial's 10-ms bins (1000 permutations), is shown as a variant at the verifier's request.

outcomes.statement: Temporally modulated units were distributed uniformly across columns and layers and had higher baseline firing rates than non-modulated units.
outcomes.source: Results, S1 Recordings during Behavioral Discrimination, paragraph 3; Figure 4C; S3B Fig
outcomes.quote: Temporally modulated units were distributed uniformly across whisker columns and layers ( Fig 4C ) and had higher baseline firing rates than non-modulated units ( S3B Fig ).
outcomes.notes: On the stored modulated set, modulated RS single units have the higher baseline in 5 of 5 layers (for example L4 10.14 against 6.55 Hz, L6 10.54 against 2.51 Hz; L5a 11.46 against 11.35 Hz). The fraction modulated is 0.49 to 0.73 across layers, chi-square p = 0.002, so on this variant layers are not uniform (p = 0.105 on the recomputed set, where the baseline is also higher in 5 of 5 layers). Columns cannot be tested, as the column map is missing.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.

outcomes.statement: The mean impulse-evoked firing rate modulation, above the pre-impulse baseline, was 14.2 Hz in L2/3, 15.2 in L4, 6.3 in L5a, 14.4 in L5b and 7.0 in L6, greatest in L2/3, L4 and L5b.
outcomes.source: Results, S1 Recordings during Behavioral Discrimination, paragraph 4; Figure 4D
outcomes.quote: The mean impulse-evoked firing rate modulation (in Hz above pre-impulse baseline) was 14.2 ± 2.3 in L2/3, 15.2 ± 1.9 in L4, 6.3 ± 1.2 in L5a, 14.4 ± 2.3 in L5b, and 7.0 ± 1.5 in L6 ( n = 28–82 units per layer).
outcomes.notes: No combination of the criterion's readings puts all five layers within tolerance. The closest, the signed peak over pooled impulses (A, a, i), gives 14.33, 14.23, 2.55, 13.11 and 5.76 Hz, 4 of 5 within tolerance (L5a outside); measured gives it. The absolute peak gives 3 of 5 or fewer and the 5 to 35 ms mean (B) 1.6 to 8.0 Hz, none. L5a and L6 are the two lowest layers under every combination. Units per layer 28 to 83. The recomputed set gives at most 3 of 5 and the same two lowest layers.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.
The 10-ms boxcar is centred, a standard choice; the segments now extend to 50 ms after impulse onset, so that the smoothing needs no padding at the end of the 40-ms window.

outcomes.statement: Among impulse-responsive units, peak response latency was shortest in L4, L5a and L5b (9.8, 10.3 and 12.0 ms) and longest in L2/3 and L6 (13.8 and 16.1 ms).
outcomes.source: Results, S1 Recordings during Behavioral Discrimination, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: Among units with significant impulse responses, peak response latency was shortest in L4, L5a, and L5b (9.8, 10.3, and 12.0 ms) and longest in L2/3 and L6 (13.8 and 16.1 ms).
outcomes.notes: With the centred 10-ms boxcar, latencies of impulse-responsive units on the stored modulated set are 15 to 22 ms in every layer, longer than the paper's 9.8 to 16.1 ms, and no layer is within tolerance. The ordering (L4, L5a and L5b below L2/3 and L6) holds for the mean and the median with the two-sided test and not with the one-sided test, where L5a is among the latest. Measured gives the two-sided centred means, the reading the partial outcome rests on, in the claim's order (L4, L5a, L5b, L2/3, L6); the one-sided medians are 15, 19, 15, 17 and 21 ms. 21 to 48 impulse-responsive units per layer. Placing the boxcar forward (t to t+9 ms) shortens latencies by about 5 ms and puts at most 2 of 5 layers within tolerance (3 on the recomputed set); the trailing boxcar puts none and the unsmoothed PSTH at most 2 (3 on the recomputed set). No reading puts all five within tolerance. Latency is now the mean of the times sharing the maximum, so that a plateau is not read at its first sample.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.
The impulse t test compares, per trial, the 5 to 35 ms rate with the 0 to 10 ms rate, averaged over the trial's three impulses, across trials (Methods, Stimulus-evoked responses, by t test).
The Methods say only 10 ms smoothing; the boxcar is centred (Matlab's smooth), a standard choice, with trailing, forward and no smoothing shown. The outcome is the same under all four.

outcomes.statement: Superimposed on the phasic impulse responses, average firing rate decreased gradually during the nose poke period in all layers except L5a.
outcomes.source: Results, S1 Recordings during Behavioral Discrimination, paragraph 4; Figure 4D
outcomes.quote: Superimposed on these phasic responses to individual impulses was a gradual decrease in average firing rate during the nose poke period, observed in all layers except L5a ( Fig 4D ).
outcomes.notes: The population rate of modulated units falls in every layer, L5a included. On the stored set the slope from -25 to 180 ms is -0.94 Hz per 100 ms in L5a (p below 0.001) and -1.42 to -2.12 in the other layers (reading a), and the last 30 ms are below the baseline in all five layers, by 1.70 Hz in L5a (reading b). The recomputed set gives the same (L5a -0.88 Hz per 100 ms). The claim requires no decrease in L5a.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.

outcomes.statement: Of the 305 temporally modulated units, 204 had a significant regression of firing rate on integrated panel speed for at least one of the 36 integration windows.
outcomes.source: Results, Regression Analysis to Identify Fast- and Slow-Time Scale Units, paragraph 1; Methods, Stimulus regression
outcomes.quote: Two hundred four units showed a significant regression for at least one stimulus integration window (α = 0.05/36 = 0.0014, using Bonferroni correction for the multiple regressions).
outcomes.notes: 207 of the 310 stored modulated units have a regression at p < 0.05/36 in at least one window (194 of the 310 units of the recomputed set). With rates per trial in place of summed counts, also 207. The fit reproduces the data set's stored R2 and p for every unit to numerical precision.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.

The regressor is the data set's stored integrated speed (Xval), the stimulus record the criterion allows; the dependent variable is the spike count summed over completed trials, as the stored inputs show.

outcomes.statement: Units were classed by best-fit integration window as Fast (5 to 20 ms, 158 units, 52%, positive slopes), Medium (25 to 55 ms, 52 units, largely negative slopes), Slow Positive (51) and Slow Negative (44); 44% of units had very fast (5 to 10 ms) windows.
outcomes.source: Results, Regression Analysis to Identify Fast- and Slow-Time Scale Units, paragraphs 2 and 3; Figure 6E; Discussion, Stimulus Encoding in S1, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Empirically, units with 5–20 ms best integration windows (Fast units; n = 158) had positive slopes. Units with 25–55 ms integration windows were rarer (Medium units; n = 52) and had largely negative slopes. Units with slow (55–180 ms) integration windows had either positive regression slope (Slow Positive units; n = 51) or negative regression slope (Slow Negative units; n = 44).
outcomes.notes: Classing all stored modulated units by their highest-R2 window (reading a) gives 160 Fast, 52 Medium, 51 Slow Positive and 47 Slow Negative with 55 ms Slow, and 160, 53, 51 and 46 with 55 ms Medium; all within tolerance, with 51.6% Fast and 43.5% with 5 to 10 ms windows. 94% of Fast units have positive slopes and 69 to 70% of Medium units negative. Reading b (significant units only) gives 125, 30 or 31, 28, 24 or 23, outside tolerance. With 55 ms Medium the classes equal the data set's labels unit for unit. On the recomputed modulated set Slow Negative is 50 or 51, above its limit of 48.4 (the first run's partial outcome), so the outcome rests on the unit set.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.

outcomes.statement: Fast units were 73% of temporally modulated units in L2/3 and L4, 50% in L5 and 23% in L6; slow units were 13% in L2/3 and L4, 31% in L5 and 56% in L6.
outcomes.source: Results, Regression Analysis to Identify Fast- and Slow-Time Scale Units, paragraph 3; Figure 6F and 6G
outcomes.quote: Fast units were 73% of temporally modulated units in L2/3 and L4, 50% in L5, and 23% in L6. ... Overall, slow units were 13% of temporally responsive units in L2/3 and L4, 31% in L5 and 56% in L6.
outcomes.notes: Under reading a on the stored modulated set, 6 of 6 values are within tolerance (Fast 74.0, 49.6 and 23.2%; Slow 13.0, 32.6 and 56.5% with 55 ms Slow, 31.9% in L5 with 55 ms Medium) and Fast falls and Slow rises from superficial to deep. Separately, L2/3 is 75.0% Fast and L4 73.6%. On the recomputed set 4 of 6 are within tolerance (L6 Fast 26.5%, L2/3 and L4 Slow 18.3%), so the outcome rests on the unit set.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.

outcomes.statement: In Fast units the evoked rate after an impulse was greater for F than S impulses and intermediate for M impulses.
outcomes.source: Results, Fast and Medium Time Scale Units, paragraph 2; Figure 7C left
outcomes.quote: The firing rate of Fast units ( n = 158) in a brief window after each impulse was greater for F versus S impulses, and intermediate for M impulses ( Fig 7C , left).
outcomes.notes: Over 160 Fast units the net evoked rate is 9.99 Hz for F, 8.54 for M and 7.77 for S impulses (SEM 0.75 to 0.88); paired t F against S, t = 4.47, p = 1.5e-05. The recomputed set gives 9.59, 8.73 and 7.42 Hz. In 18Ri M is above F and in 107St S above M.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.

outcomes.statement: Mean firing rate of Fast units over the whole sequence (0 to 150 ms) followed the mean speed of the sequence, highest for FFF, lowest for SSS, and intermediate and equal for FMS and SMF.
outcomes.source: Results, Fast and Medium Time Scale Units, paragraph 2; Figure 7C right
outcomes.quote: Mean firing rate measured over the entire duration of a sequence (0–150 ms after sequence onset) varied closely with mean speed of the sequence, being highest for FFF, lowest for SSS, and intermediate and equal for FMS and SMF ( Fig 7C , right).
outcomes.notes: With the 25-ms baseline (reading a) Fast units give FFF 4.10, FMS 2.68, SMF 3.56 and SSS 1.59 Hz above baseline, FMS against SMF p = 0.058; with the 0 to 10 ms baseline (reading b) 4.75, 2.28, 3.19 and 1.63 Hz, p = 0.234. The claim holds under both. On the recomputed set FMS and SMF differ at p = 0.046 with the 25-ms baseline.
deviations: Temporally modulated units are the data set's own (TempSig.TemporalPval < 0.05), which the data descriptor names as the units of the paper's analyses; the set recomputed with the Methods' test has the same count but agrees for 73% of units and is shown as a variant. Classes are recomputed from the regression (reading a, 55 ms Medium) and equal the data set's labels. Changed from the recomputed set after the verifier's first report.

outcomes.statement: Fast RS single units adapted modestly in FFF trains, with pulse 2 to pulse 1 ratio 0.80 and pulse 3 to pulse 1 ratio 0.70, significant by t test.
outcomes.source: Results, Fast and Medium Time Scale Units, paragraph 1; S4 Fig
outcomes.quote: Adaptation within each train was quantified as mean firing rate to pulse N/pulse 1 and was modest in FFF trains (2/1: 0.80 ± 0.11, 3/1: 0.70 ± 0.14, p < 0.05 by t test, n = 61 single RS units with significant response to F impulses)

statistics.n: 61 Fast RS single units with significant response to F impulses

outcomes.notes: The impulse t test selects 29 to 37 of the 62 Fast RS single units (one-sided 37, two-sided 34, first impulse only 29), not 61, and on those no combination meets the criterion (ratios of means within tolerance, paired p 0.04 to 0.28). All 62 Fast RS single units, the selection closest to the paper's 61, give ratios of population means of 0.744 (2/1) and 0.663 (3/1), within tolerance, with paired t tests p = 0.037 and 0.013 (25-ms baseline; 0.779 and 0.709 with the same p for the 0 to 10 ms baseline), which meets the criterion under (b, ii). The mean of per-unit ratios (pulse 1 above 1 Hz) is outside tolerance for 2/1 (0.42 and 0.65). On the recomputed set the 63 Fast RS units give 0.701 and 0.773, p = 0.039 and 0.141.

findings.statement: The data descriptor gives the column of each electrode as AllRats(expt).MapPosition and says units in columns A1 and B2 must not be used in stimulus analyses, but AllRats.mat has no MapPosition field. No field gives the recorded column.

AllRats.mat holds 506 units (330 single, 176 multi-unit) where the paper reports 473 (306 single, 167 multi-unit). The extra units are probably those in columns A1 and B2, but without the column map they cannot be identified, so every unit analysis here uses all 506. Against the unit counts per layer and type of the paper's S1 Table, the extra units are in L2/3 (4), L4 (8), L5a (15) and L5b (6), none in L6.

The data set holds only the five recorded rats. The fixed-panel control sessions and the behaviour of rats 62SC, 107Si and 62SS (Figure 2) are not deposited; the paper's S1 and S2 Data give only per-rat and per-session summaries.

The stored regression inputs (StimReg Yval) equal the spike counts summed over completed trials (Complete equal to 1) for all 506 units, while the descriptor says the paper used trials with nose poke duration over 250 ms, a set that also holds 129 trials without a choice. The stored regression results are reproduced exactly from the spikes and the stored regressor.

For rat 18FB the per-rat right-choice fractions computed from the data set's sessions differ by up to 0.026 from the S1 Data values of Figure 2B, while for the other four rats they are equal, so S1 Data and the data set hold different sessions for 18FB.

verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebooks of the author-revise-1 run (reproduce_mcguire_2016.ipynb and decoders.ipynb), the helper module ssc4.py, the claims file and this record, with the paper. Report in transcripts/mcguire-2016/verifier-2-report.md. The verifier agrees with all 37 outcomes, found again no place where the claims file misreads the paper, and found that each assumed outcome states its assumption reasonably. It quoted six places where the text did not match the printed outputs (fig9f cross-validated values and unweighted range, latency-by-layer measured, fig8d-fast-medium times, fig9d first-run value, baseline-rates deviations), listed B1 and B3 to B11 as resolved, and named five remaining points that bear on a conclusion (the 62 Fast RS units of fig7-fff-adaptation, the unit-set dependence of seven outcomes, the s5 impulse speeds, the weak support of fig9e, and fig9d at the edge of its band).

paper_notes.statement: Question for the authors. The stored temporal-modulation p-values (TempSig) were computed over -50 to 300 ms in 10-ms bins (TempSig.Params), while the Methods give 0 to 180 ms after nose poke entry, and the Methods do not name the statistic compared with permuted spikes. Permuting spikes uniformly and comparing the PSTH variance gives 310 modulated units over the Methods' window, the same count as the stored values, but the two agree for only 73% of units (82% with the stored window, and 82% with the stored window and a null that shuffles each trial's 10-ms bins). Which window and statistic were used for the paper's 305?

Question for the authors. Which test selected the 61 Fast RS single units with significant response to F impulses? A paired t test across trials of the 5 to 35 ms rate against the 0 to 10 ms rate selects 29 to 37 of the 62 Fast RS single units of the data set's classes (one-sided, two-sided, or first impulses only); the paper's 61 is close to all of them.

Question for the authors. How was the choice decoder's 65% obtained? With per-unit logistic functions summed over a pseudo-population, as the Methods describe, Slow units give 81 to 93% when the two choices are weighted equally in training and about 54% when they are not, and Fast/Medium units 71 to 82%. Accuracy grows with the number of units (about 66 to 74% with 20 Slow units). Were the choices balanced, how many units entered each prediction, and were test trials drawn within each rat?

Question for the authors. How were the peak latency and the evoked modulation of Figure 4D computed (placement of the 10-ms smoothing window, pooling of impulses and sequences)? From the centred 10-ms smoothed 1-ms PSTH the latencies are 15 to 22 ms in every layer, against 9.8 to 16.1 ms in the paper; a forward window shortens them by about 5 ms but still puts at most 2 or 3 of 5 layers within 10%.

In S1 Data the Figure 2A sheet is labelled "Rat 107ST", but its values are those of 107Si in the same file and in S2 Data. Its mean FFF fraction over 13 days is 0.7485, the Figure 2B mean of 107Si (0.7485, 107ST 0.5856), and its fixed-panel FFF minus SSS (0.0991, d-prime 0.277) equals 107SI in S2B Fig and 107Si in Figure 2D. The example rat of Figure 2A appears to be 107Si.

entries.name: mcguire-2016
entries.title: Short time-scale coding in rat S1 during whisker sequence discrimination (McGuire et al. 2016)
entries.description: Tests the findings of McGuire, Telian, Laboy-Juarez et al. (2016) on CRCNS ssc-4, which holds the spike times and trial data of 80 recording sessions in the five recorded rats. It checks the behaviour of those rats, the unit counts, baseline rates, temporal modulation, impulse responses by layer, the regression on integrated panel speed that classes units as Fast, Medium, Slow Positive and Slow Negative, the responses and choice coding of each class, and the population decoders of stimulus and choice. Three claims are tested on the paper's supporting data.
